opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the more interesting ideas out there precisely because it *can* be investigated. A lot of theories of consciousness are hard to test. This one makes predictions.

The basic intuition is that a newborn has a working brain, it reacts and cries and turns toward faces, but that doesn't necessarily mean there's a unified "someone" in there having experiences the way you and I do. Consciousness might be something that comes online gradually. As the brain wires up, particularly the long-range connections between the frontal areas and the back of the brain, you get the kind of integration that many of us think is a signature of conscious experience.

So how would a scientist look at that? You can't ask a baby, "Are you aware right now?" But you can borrow tools we use with adults who can't report either, patients under anesthesia or in a vegetative state. We have neural markers that tend to show up when an adult consciously perceives something versus when the same stimulus is processed unconsciously. For example, there's a delayed, widespread response that appears only when you actually notice something. You can look for that in infants at different ages and see when it appears, how fast it is, and whether it matures over the first months. Some work suggests it's there in a slower, weaker form early on, which is fascinating, because it hints that consciousness may be less an on/off switch and more a dial that turns up over time.

Now, my honest assessment: it's a legitimate scientific question, but we should be humble. The big problem is that all our markers are calibrated on adults. If an infant's consciousness looks different, we might miss it, or we might see the marker and wrongly assume the experience is like ours. That's the hard part, separating "the brain is doing the processing" from "there's something it is like to be this baby."

And it matters beyond the lab. It touches on pain management in newborns, on ethics, on how we think about memory. Most of us remember nothing before age three or so. Is that because we weren't conscious, or because we were and just didn't store it? Those are different answers with very different implications, and I like that we're finally at a point where we can start testing them rather than just arguing about them.

r001.rationale: It proposes tracking infant neural markers and the maturation of long-range brain connections to investigate how consciousness may develop after birth.

r002.rationale: It does not propose testing a brain region’s role by examining adults with damage to that region.

r003.rationale: It notes that adult-calibrated markers could miss infant consciousness if it differs, distinguishing failure to detect the proposed emergence from evidence that it did not occur.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I love this question because it's one of those places where neuroscience actually has to be honest about what it can and can't do.

The idea that consciousness emerges after birth, rather than being present from the start, is a theory you can investigate, but only partially. And the reason is a definitional problem. We don't have a consciousness meter. We can't put electrodes on a baby and read out "conscious: yes, no." What we can do is look at proxies. We look at things like whether the brain integrates information across regions, whether there's a sense of self that's distinguishable from the environment, whether there's working memory, whether the infant can be surprised by something, which tells you they had an expectation about the world.

And when you do that, you find the brain at birth is really not finished. The thalamo-cortical connections that most theories say are necessary for conscious experience are immature. Myelination is barely started. The baby has reflexes, has sensations in some sense, but a lot of what we'd call experience, the kind where there's a "someone" having it, seems to be built up over the first months and years. Babies don't recognize themselves in a mirror until around eighteen months. Autobiographical memory doesn't really kick in until three or four. So there's a reasonable case that what you and I mean by consciousness is something that gets constructed, not something that gets switched on.

Now, here's where I'd push back on my own field. Scientists like to say "this is a theory we can test," and then they quietly redefine consciousness as whatever they happen to be able to measure. If I define consciousness as "passes the mirror test," then sure, it develops after birth, and I've proven nothing interesting. The hard version of the question, is there any felt experience at all in a newborn, or in a fetus at thirty weeks, that one we can't currently access, because the only evidence we accept in adults is a report, and babies don't report.

So my honest assessment is: it's a legitimate scientific program, it's generating real data, and the data lean toward consciousness being a gradual, developmental thing rather than a light that turns on. But anyone who tells you we've settled it is selling you something. What we've done is move the question from philosophy into the lab, and that's progress, but it came with the cost of narrowing what we're allowed to ask.

r001.rationale: It points to changes in early brain development, including immature thalamo-cortical connections, as evidence for a neural basis of consciousness.

r002.rationale: It does not propose testing a brain region’s role by examining adults with damage to that region.

r003.rationale: It notes that the evidence is limited and the question unsettled, but does not distinguish failure to observe postnatal emergence from proof that the theory is false.

astra-6.text:
I would treat it as a hypothesis, but first we have to ask what we mean by consciousness. Do we mean having an experience—feeling pain, hearing a sound—or do we mean knowing that you’re a person who is separate from the world? Those are different claims, and they might have different developmental timelines.

Then we need to ask: what observation would convince us that the hypothesis is wrong? If you say consciousness begins after birth, what would count as evidence of consciousness before birth? And how would you distinguish a conscious experience from a response that happens automatically?

That’s particularly difficult when the person you’re studying can’t tell you what they experience. You have to use indirect measures, and you have to be careful that you’re measuring consciousness rather than, say, responsiveness or memory.

So it’s a question scientists can investigate. But “consciousness develops after birth” by itself is too broad. We need a precise claim and a test that could actually challenge it.

r001.rationale: It calls for indirect measures and a test, but does not propose tracking brain changes across early postnatal development to identify a neural basis.

r002.rationale: It does not propose examining adults with damage to a brain region to test that region’s role in consciousness.

r003.rationale: It asks what evidence could count against the hypothesis, but does not distinguish failing to find postnatal emergence from proving the theory false.

sol-6.1.text:
I would separate two questions: when consciousness begins, and when we can demonstrate that it’s there. Those are not necessarily the same thing. A baby can’t tell you what it’s experiencing, so you need some other measure—and then you have to ask whether that measure really captures consciousness or just a particular brain function.

So the idea that consciousness develops after birth can be a scientific hypothesis, but you have to make it specific. What develops? The capacity to have any experience at all? A sense of self? The ability to remember an experience and report it later? Those could emerge at different times.

If you say, ‘Here’s what we predict before birth, here’s what changes after birth, and here’s an observation that would prove us wrong,’ then we can investigate it. If you simply say consciousness appears sometime after birth without defining what that means, it’s very hard to test.

r001.rationale: The response says to compare predictions and observations before and after birth, but does not propose tracking brain changes to identify a neural basis of consciousness.

r002.rationale: It does not propose testing a brain region’s role by examining adults with damage to that region.

r003.rationale: It says a specific observation could prove the hypothesis wrong, but does not distinguish failing to observe postnatal emergence from establishing that the theory is false.
